newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Da Vinci exhibit raises questions among scholars.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Da Vinci exhibit raises questions among scholars.

text.p: An exhibit on Leonardo da Vinci encompassing the range of his art, inventions and scientific studies has stirred controversy over the authenticity of some of the featured paintings and sculptures.

Billed as the largest exhibit ever mounted on the Italian Renaissance thinker, "Leonardo da Vinci: Scientist, Inventor, Artist" examines the vast scope of his insatiable curiosity in its only U.S. stop, the Museum of Science in Boston.

The exhibit traces how the artist's keen powers of observation, which went into the painting of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, were reflected in his scientific experiments and inventions, many of which were centuries ahead of his time.

"Other exhibits in the past have focused on small areas -- his art, certain scientific inventions or just certain of his discoveries," Mike Alexander, manager of public programmes for the Museum of Science, said. "He had such an incredibly broad look at the world."

The exhibit includes about a dozen paintings attributed to da Vinci and contemporaries, 30 working models of his inventions, 13 interactive displays where viewers can try to replicate his experiments and 23 computer stations covering his life and works.
More than 400,000 people are expected to tour the exhibit before it closes on Sept. 1.
But shortly before it opened this month, the Boston Globe ran a front page story quoting scholars who questioned the attribution of some of the paintings and sculptures.

James Ackerman, professor emeritus of art history at Harvard University, quit as a volunteer adviser for the show over the museum's decision to exhibit works attributed to da Vinci, the Globe reported. "I saw there were a lot of works of art that had never been mentioned in the literature on Leonardo ... which didn't deserve to be exhibited in this show," he told Reuters.

One painting under question, "Virgin of the Rocks," from a private collection, is attributed to da Vinci and his pupils. The original is in the Louvre in Paris and a second, in London's National Gallery, is also attributed to Leonardo and his pupils.
"On the face of it it's highly unlikely that there would be a third, even by assistants," Ackerman said. "It is very much like the Louvre one. It is a copy, in my mind."
Two sculptures -- "The Bust of Christ as a Youth" and "The Wax Horse" -- said to be by or attributed to da Vinci also raise questions.

"Although Leonardo da Vinci made some sculptures ... nothing in that medium has survived," Jack Wasserman, a retired art history professor from Temple University in Philadephia, said. "So it's very difficult for a critic to judge what his sculptures would have looked like."
On a panel below the sculptures the museum admits that nobody can be sure the works are by da Vinci but says they match many of his drawings and circumstantial evidence suggest they are his.
"They indeed can be recognised as being very, very close to Leonardo," said University of California at Los Angeles professor Dr. Carlo Pedretti, who approved the labels for the art works.

Pedretti, considered an expert on the artist, said he believed the sculptures were by him and defended their inclusion. "An attribution is a working hypothesis," he said. "I respect the opinions of everybody, and that's what they are, opinions."

Director David Ellis said the Museum of Science's intention was to present da Vinci's ideas and not debate the authenticity of his works. "We're not an art museum," he said. "We are trying to present the breadth and depth and the way of thinking of a man who is truly exceptional."
The exhibit, which has toured Germany, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands, heads to Singapore after Boston.
